name: Steam
tagline: PC game store, DRM, library manager and social layer rolled into one client.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. The client is free, spend is per game purchase.

verdictSummary: An agent can absolutely build you a launcher: scan folders, show cover art, track playtime, launch executables. What it cannot build is the right to the games, and that is the entire product. Steam is a two-sided market where the catalog exists because publishers signed with Valve and the buyers are there because the catalog is, plus a decade of purchase history, cloud saves, workshop mods and friend lists welded to one account. Even the parts that look like software, the offline DRM handshake and the content delivery network shoving terabytes at millions of concurrent users, are infrastructure problems, not weekend problems. Build the launcher if your library is scattered across GOG, itch and random installers. Do not expect to build the store.
coreLoopDIY: Scans local folders for game executables, pulls in cover art and notes you supply, launches them and logs playtime to a local SQLite file.
requirements: Games you already own and can legally run outside a store client
A machine to run the launcher on, Windows or Linux
Cover art and metadata you provide or scrape yourself
whatYouLose: The store: no catalog, no purchases, no licenses to anything you do not already own
Cloud saves and cross-machine sync of progress
Friends, chat, reviews, Workshop mods and community pages
Automatic patching and multi-gigabyte downloads at high speed
Achievements, controller remapping, Big Picture, family sharing and every other thing Valve quietly ships
moatNotes: Valve's leverage is contractual and social, not technical. The launcher is the least interesting part of Steam.
whyPeopleStillPay: People do not pay for the Steam client, they pay for games inside it, and that is exactly why the moat holds. The catalog is licensed, the purchase history is a decade of sunk cost, and the friend list is where the co-op sessions get organised. A local launcher can tidy up a scattered library and it is a genuinely nice thing to have, but it cannot sell you Baldur's Gate 3, cannot restore a save on a fresh install, and cannot tell you which of your friends is online right now. The switching cost is not the software, it is everything you already bought.
notes: A launcher is an evening; a licensed catalog is not. The moat is content rights plus twenty years of purchase history and friend lists nobody wants to abandon.
prompt:
Build a local-only PC game launcher and playtime tracker. No store, no accounts, no cloud.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Tauri 2 with a React + TypeScript + Vite frontend
- Rust backend for filesystem scanning and process launching
- SQLite via rusqlite, database file stored in the app data directory
- Tailwind for styling, no component library

Features in scope:
1. Library folders: user adds one or more directories. Recursive scan finds candidate game executables (.exe on Windows, executable files and .sh on Linux). Ignore obvious noise: unins*, vcredist, dxsetup, crash handlers, anything inside a directory named redist or _CommonRedist.
2. Each detected game becomes a row: title guessed from the parent folder name, path, platform, date added. User can rename, hide, or merge duplicates.
3. Cover art: user drops an image onto a game card, or pastes a local file path. Store copies in an app-managed covers directory. No external API calls, no scraping.
4. Launch: clicking play spawns the executable with its own working directory, records start time, and records end time when the process exits. Handle the case where the process forks and exits immediately by tracking a configurable child process name per game.
5. Playtime: total hours, last played, session history per game. A simple bar chart of the last 30 days.
6. Filters and sort: by name, last played, total playtime, hidden. Text search.
7. Tags: freeform tags per game, filter by tag.
8. Export: dump the whole library and session log to JSON on demand.

Explicitly out of scope: purchasing anything, DRM, patch downloads, cloud saves, friends, achievements, metadata scraping from third-party APIs, telemetry.

No secrets are needed. Do not create a .env unless you add something that genuinely requires a key.

Deliver: working app, README with build and run steps for Windows and Linux, and a seed script that inserts three fake games so the UI can be checked without a real library.
